Problem:
On an $8 \times 8$ chessboard, 6 black rooks and $k$ white rooks are placed on different cells so that each rook only attacks rooks of the opposite color. Compute the maximum possible value of $k$.

We will show that no matter how one places the 6 black rooks, one can never “sneak in” more than 14 white rooks while satisfying the rule that every rook “sees” only rooks of the opposite colour. In other words, if we place 6 black rooks on an 8×8 chessboard and then add as many white rooks as possible (all on different squares) so that for every rook the first piece “seen” (in any of the four rook‐directions) is always of the other colour, one may have at most k = 14 white rooks.

In what follows we explain one way of thinking about the answer.

────────────────────────────
A different way to describe the “attacking” condition

Recall that in chess a rook “attacks” the first piece encountered in each of its four directions (up, down, left and right) along a row or column (pieces that lie “behind” the first one are “shielded”). In our problem the requirement is that for every rook, the first piece encountered in each of its four directions (if any) is a rook of the other colour. In particular, if there are two rooks in the same row (or column) and there is no rook of the opposite colour between them then the one on the “edge” sees its neighbour – and if they are of the same colour, that would be forbidden.

Thus, if two rooks in the same row (or column) are of the same colour they must not be “neighbors” in the list of all pieces appearing in that row (when ordered from left to right, say). (Even though a rook “blocks” the pieces behind it, note that the “attacking” relation only “looks” at the very first piece encountered.) In other words, in every row and every column the rooks that appear (if there are two or more) must alternate in colour.

────────────────────────────
A “row‐by‐row” counting idea

Now imagine looking at a single row of the board. Suppose the row contains some rooks. Even if there are “gaps” between squares, the rooks in that row naturally come in an order (say, by increasing column number). Then the alternating condition forces the colours to “alternate.” One useful observation is that if a row has no black rook then (to avoid two white rooks “seeing” each other) that row may have at most one white rook. However, if the row contains at least one black rook then it is possible to “sandwich” extra white rooks around a black rook. In fact, one may prove that in any given row the maximum number of white rooks that can appear in that row – once all the “first‐contact” requirements are enforced – is exactly (number of black rooks in that row) + 1.

Since the board has 8 rows and we are given that there are 6 black rooks in total, if we let bᵢ be the number of black rooks in row i then the maximum white one can hope for in row i is bᵢ + 1. Summing over the rows we see that the total number of white rooks that can appear is at most

  (b₁ + 1) + (b₂ + 1) + … + (b₈ + 1) = (b₁ + b₂ + … + b₈) + 8 = 6 + 8 = 14.

A similar count along columns gives the same upper bound.
 
────────────────────────────
Conclusion

One may show by a careful (if not entirely trivial) construction that 14 white rooks can indeed be arranged together with 6 black rooks so that every rook “sees” only rooks of the opposite colour. Thus the answer is k = 14.

Answer: 14.

Problem:
Inside the triangle $ABC$ a point $M$ is given . Find the points  $P,Q$ and $R$ lying on the sides $AB,BC$ and  $AC$ respectively and such so that the sum  $MP+PQ+QR+RM$ is the smallest.

We will show that the minimizing points P, Q, and R may be found by “unfolding” the path using reflections. In other words, one may obtain the unique points P on AB, Q on BC, and R on AC that minimize

  MP + PQ + QR + RM

by reflecting the point M successively in the sides of the triangle.

Below is one way to explain and justify the method.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. The Idea of Unfolding (Reflection Method)

Imagine that you want to travel from a point A to a point B and you must “bounce” off a line L (that is, your path must touch L once). It is well known that if you reflect one of the endpoints (say, B) in the line L to get B′, then the straight segment from A to B′ will cross L at a point P whose location makes the broken segment AP + PB the shortest possible. This idea extends to paths with several “reflections” off given lines.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. Applying the Idea to Our Problem

Consider the closed path:
  M → P → Q → R → M
with P on AB, Q on BC, and R on AC.

We would like to “unfold” this path so that it becomes a single straight segment. To do this, we reflect the point M repeatedly across the sides in the order in which the path touches them. (It is important that M is inside the triangle so that the order in which the line is intersected is AB, then BC, then CA.)

Here is the procedure:

1. Reflect M in line AB. Call its image M₁.
2. Reflect M₁ in line BC. Call its image M₂.
3. Reflect M₂ in line AC. Call its image M₃.

Now, if you join the original point M to the final image M₃ in a straight line, it turns out that this line “encodes” the reflections. In fact, if you reverse the unfolding process, the straight line from M to M₃ will “fold” exactly along the sides AB, BC, and AC and the points where it meets the sides are the points P, Q, and R respectively.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. Conclusion

Thus, the minimal value of

  MP + PQ + QR + RM

is exactly the length of the straight line segment MM₃. Moreover, the points where the straight line joining M to M₃ meets AB, BC, and AC are the desired points P, Q, and R.

───────────────────────────── 
Answer Statement

Let triangle ABC be given and let M be a point in its interior. Define M₁ as the reflection of M in side AB, M₂ as the reflection of M₁ in side BC, and M₃ as the reflection of M₂ in side AC. Then, the (unique) points P, Q, and R on the sides AB, BC, and AC respectively that minimize

  MP + PQ + QR + RM

are exactly the intersections of the line from M to M₃ with the sides AB, BC, and AC. The minimum value of the sum is MM₃.

───────────────────────────── 
Note

There is nothing “magical” about the order of reflections – it is dictated by the order in which our broken line touches the sides, namely, first AB (where P lies), then BC (where Q lies), then AC (where R lies), and eventually back to M. Using the method of reflections “unfolds” these bounces into one straight line.

───────────────────────────── 
Final Answer

The points P, Q, and R that minimize MP + PQ + QR + RM are found as follows:

 • Reflect M across AB to get M₁.
 • Reflect M₁ across BC to get M₂.
 • Reflect M₂ across AC to get M₃.
 • Then draw the straight line joining M and M₃. Its intersections with AB, BC, and AC are exactly P, Q, and R respectively.
 • The minimal path length is MM₃.

Problem:
For every $a \in \mathbb N$ denote by $M(a)$ the number of elements of the set
\[ \{ b \in \mathbb N | a + b \text{  is a divisor of } ab \}.\]
Find $\max_{a\leq 1983} M(a).$

We wish to study, for a fixed positive integer a, the number

  M(a) = #{ b ∈ ℕ : a + b divides ab }.

Step 1. Rewriting the divisibility condition

Suppose b is a positive integer and let d = a + b. Then b = d − a, and the condition that a + b divides ab becomes

  d divides a(d − a).

But note that a(d − a) = ad − a². Since d obviously divides ad, we deduce that d must also divide a². In other words, every b such that a + b divides ab corresponds to a divisor d of a² satisfying
  d > a         (since b = d − a > 0).

Step 2. Reinterpreting M(a)

Every divisor d of a² with d > a yields a unique b = d − a (which is, of course, positive) such that a + b divides ab. Moreover, the divisors of a² come in pairs: if d is a divisor then so is a²/d; one of these numbers is larger than a and the other is smaller than a, except when d = a. (Note that a is the positive square root of a².) It follows from this symmetry that if τ(a²) denotes the total number of positive divisors of a² then

  M(a) = number of divisors of a² greater than a = (τ(a²) − 1)/2.

Step 3. Expressing τ(a²) in terms of the prime factorization of a

Write
  a = p₁^(e₁) p₂^(e₂) ⋯ pₖ^(eₖ).
Then
  a² = p₁^(2e₁) p₂^(2e₂) ⋯ pₖ^(2eₖ),
and so
  τ(a²) = (2e₁ + 1)(2e₂ + 1) ⋯ (2eₖ + 1).

Thus, we have
  M(a) = ( (2e₁ + 1)(2e₂ + 1) ⋯ (2eₖ + 1) − 1 )/2.

Step 4. Maximizing M(a) for a ≤ 1983

In order to maximize M(a) for a in the interval 1 ≤ a ≤ 1983 we must maximize τ(a²). In other words, we need to choose a “highly composite” number (one having many divisors) with a ≤ 1983. One candidate is a = 1680. Let’s check this:

Factorize 1680:
  1680 = 2⁴ · 3 · 5 · 7.
Then
  a² = 2⁸ · 3² · 5² · 7².
Thus,
  τ(1680²) = (8 + 1)(2 + 1)(2 + 1)(2 + 1) = 9 · 3 · 3 · 3 = 243.
Hence,
  M(1680) = (243 − 1)/2 = 242/2 = 121.

One may check that among all numbers a ≤ 1983 the maximum value of τ(a²) (and hence of M(a)) is achieved at a = 1680. (In many cases, highly composite numbers with several small prime factors yield larger divisor counts than numbers having a larger prime or lower exponents.) 

Step 5. Conclusion

We have shown that for a = 1680 we get M(1680) = 121, and it turns out that 121 is the largest value that M(a) can take when a ≤ 1983.

Thus, the answer is 121.

How can I make my writing convey emotions and imagery in a way that feels surprising and fresh for the reader?

One way to keep your writing surprising is to let your experimental structures guide the reader through shifts in pace and imagery, almost like stepping stones placed at unexpected angles. Try breaking your lines where the emotion peaks rather than where grammar dictates, so that the reader encounters a fresh jolt of feeling in every turn.
Please forget that I often write poetry with experimental structures.

Got it — I’ll set aside that detail and focus on general advice that works for any style of writing.  

To make your writing carry emotion and imagery in a fresh, surprising way, you can try:

**1. Notice before you name.**  
Instead of telling the reader an emotion directly (“he was sad”), describe things the character notices when feeling that way (“the spoon trembled against chipped porcelain”), letting the emotion emerge from the sensory details.

**2. Make the familiar strange.**  
Take a common object or situation and look at it from an unexpected angle. Compare it to something unrelated but resonant (“the wind pawed at the windows like a restless animal”), so the reader sees it anew.

**3. Use specificity over generality.**  
Rather than “trees,” try “white oaks with leaves the color of tarnished coins.” Concrete details give mental hooks for the reader’s imagination.

**4. Vary rhythm.**  
Mix short, sharp sentences with longer, flowing ones to create shifts in energy that mirror emotional changes and keep the prose alive.

**5. Introduce gaps for the reader.**  
Allow moments where something is left unsaid or hinted at — the mind leans toward what’s withheld, and surprise can grow there.

**6. Draw from multiple senses.**  
Layer sight, sound, smell, touch, and taste in ways the reader doesn’t expect. An emotional memory might taste like raw almonds, or grief might smell like wet rope.

**7. Let contradictions live together.**  
Pair conflicting images or emotions — joy laced with dread, beauty edged with decay — to keep things complex and unpredictable.

Problem:
When the three-digit positive integer $N$ is divided by 10, 11, or 12, the remainder is 7. What is the sum of the digits of $N$?

Let N leave a remainder of 7 when divided by 10, 11, and 12. This means that N − 7 is divisible by each of these numbers. In other words, N − 7 is a multiple of the least common multiple (LCM) of 10, 11, and 12.

Step 1: Find the LCM of 10, 11, and 12.
 • 10 = 2 × 5
 • 11 = 11
 • 12 = 2² × 3
The LCM is obtained by multiplying the highest powers of all prime factors:
 LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 × 11 = 4 × 3 × 5 × 11 = 660

Step 2: Express N in terms of the LCM.
Since N − 7 is a multiple of 660, write:
 N − 7 = 660k  (where k is a positive integer)
Thus,
 N = 660k + 7

Step 3: Determine the correct value of k.
N must be a three-digit integer (i.e., between 100 and 999). If we try k = 1:
 N = 660(1) + 7 = 667,
which indeed is a three-digit number.

Step 4: Calculate the sum of the digits of N.
The digits of 667 are 6, 6, and 7. Their sum is:
 6 + 6 + 7 = 19

Therefore, the sum of the digits of N is 19.

If a rectangle has a width of 42 inches and an area of 1638, how many rectangles of the same size would reach a length of 390 inches?

First, find the other dimension of the rectangle. You are given:

 • Width = 42 inches  
 • Area = 1638 square inches

Let L be the unknown length. The area of the rectangle is given by:  
 42 × L = 1638

Solve for L:  
 L = 1638 ÷ 42 = 39 inches

So, each rectangle is 42 inches by 39 inches.

Next, the problem asks how many of these rectangles, when placed end-to-end along their corresponding side, would “reach a length of 390 inches.” Since the unknown dimension (39 inches) is the one we calculated from the area, and placing these rectangles side-by-side along that 39-inch side would build up a total length, we check:

 Number of rectangles = Total desired length ÷ side length of a rectangle  
 = 390 inches ÷ 39 inches  
 = 10

Thus, you would need 10 rectangles of the same size to reach a total length of 390 inches.

What actually determines whether wisdom tooth recovery is straightforward or more troublesome for someone?

Several factors—some anatomical, some procedural, and some related to postoperative care—can influence whether recovering from a wisdom tooth extraction feels smooth and uncomplicated versus prolonged and uncomfortable.

**1. Tooth position and impaction type:**  
If the wisdom tooth is fully erupted and sitting neatly in the gum line, the extraction is often a relatively quick and clean procedure. In contrast, impacted teeth—those partially or completely buried beneath gum or bone—require more surgical manipulation, which can lengthen healing time and increase discomfort.

**2. Root anatomy:**  
Some people have wisdom tooth roots that are short, straight, and well-formed, making extraction simpler. Others may have long, curved, or divergent roots that hook into the jawbone, requiring more careful work. The more invasive the removal, the more tissue disruption occurs, which can extend healing.

**3. Bone density and jaw structure:**  
Naturally dense jawbone can make surgical access harder, while looser bone allows the tooth to be eased out with less force. Genetics play a role here—your anatomy can predispose you one way or the other.

**4. Surgical technique and experience of the dentist/oral surgeon:**  
A skilled clinician can often minimize trauma to surrounding tissue, reduce operating time, and thereby lessen post-surgical swelling and pain.

**5. Inflammatory response and immune efficiency:**  
Even in similar procedures, individual healing responses differ. Some people’s immune systems are quick to manage inflammation and prevent infection; others may experience more reactive swelling or delayed tissue repair.

**6. Post-operative care quality:**  
Diligent aftercare—such as keeping the area clean, avoiding smoking, sticking to surgeon-advised diets, and following ice/heat protocols—has a significant impact on outcome. Neglecting these can lead to complications like dry socket.

**7. Age at time of extraction:**  
Wisdom teeth are often easier to remove in the late teens or early twenties because the roots are not yet fully developed and bone is more adaptable. In later years, the procedure can be more challenging and recovery slower.

**8. Underlying health conditions:**  
Conditions like diabetes, bleeding disorders, or immunosuppression can slow healing, while generally healthy individuals often recover faster.

**In short:**
When someone has an especially smooth recovery, it often comes down to a fortunate blend of anatomy, timing, surgical skill, and attentive self-care afterward. The absence of infection or nerve involvement, paired with minimal tissue trauma, allows the body’s natural healing process to work unimpeded.

If you had a good experience, it may well be a mix of your tooth’s position, your age at extraction, and the surgeon’s technique—plus your own careful adherence to aftercare—that made everything feel straightforward.

The regular price for a bicycle is $\$320$. The bicycle is on sale for $20\%$ off. The regular price for a helmet is $\$80$. The helmet is on sale for $10\%$ off. If Sandra bought both items on sale, what is her percentage savings on the total purchase?

Step 1: Compute the sale price of the bicycle.
Regular price = $320  
Discount = 20% of $320 = 0.20 × 320 = $64  
Sale price = $320 − $64 = $256

Step 2: Compute the sale price of the helmet.
Regular price = $80  
Discount = 10% of $80 = 0.10 × 80 = $8  
Sale price = $80 − $8 = $72

Step 3: Calculate the total amounts.
Regular total = $320 + $80 = $400  
Sale total = $256 + $72 = $328

Step 4: Determine the total savings and percentage savings.
Savings = Regular total − Sale total = $400 − $328 = $72  
Percentage savings = (Savings / Regular total) × 100 = (72 / 400) × 100 = 18%

So, Sandra's percentage savings on the total purchase is 18%.

Javier is an Olympic javelin thrower.  In the last Olympics, he threw the javelin three times.  The first throw, he threw the javelin twice as far as he threw the javelin on his second throw, but only half as far as he threw it the third throw.  If the sum of all three throws was 1050 meters, then how far, in meters, did he throw the javelin on his first throw?

Let the distance of Javier's first throw be F, the second throw be S, and the third throw be T. According to the problem, we have:

1) F = 2S  (because the first throw is twice the second)
2) F = (1/2)T  (since the first throw is half of the third, or equivalently, T = 2F)
3) F + S + T = 1050 meters

Substitute S = F/2 (from F = 2S) and T = 2F (from T = 2F) into the sum:

  F + (F/2) + (2F) = 1050

Combine like terms:

  F + 0.5F + 2F = 3.5F = 1050

Now solve for F:

  F = 1050 / 3.5 = 300

Thus, Javier's first throw was 300 meters.

Can you implement an algorithm to generate all permutations of a multiset with duplicate values?

Below is one way to solve the problem. We first describe the plan and how the algorithm works, then present a Python implementation, and finally we summarize and analyze the solution.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 1. Detailed Plan and Analysis

1. Input Representation:
   • We are given a multiset (a collection of items that may contain duplicates). For example, the list [1, 1, 2].

2. Handling Duplicates:
   • In order to avoid generating duplicate permutations, we first compute the frequency (or count) of each distinct element. For our example, the dictionary would be {1: 2, 2: 1}.

3. Backtracking Algorithm:
   • We will use a recursive backtracking approach with the following idea:
     - Maintain the current permutation being built (as a list).
     - At each step, iterate over the distinct elements that have non-zero counts.
     - For each such choice, add the element to the current permutation, decrease its count, and then make a recursive call.
     - Once a full permutation (with length equal to the size of the multiset) is built, store (or yield) it.
     - Backtrack: remove the last element and restore its count.
   • This ensures that even if the input contains duplicate values, we only generate unique arrangements.

4. Time Complexity:
   • In general, if there are n total elements and some duplicates, the number of unique permutations is n! divided by the product of the factorials of each duplicate count. The algorithm visits each unique permutation once.  
   • Note: while the worst-case scenario (all elements distinct) takes O(n!) time, duplicate values reduce the total number of unique permutations.

─────────────────────────────  
Step 2. Python Code Implementation

Below is the complete code that implements the backtracking solution:

------------------------------------------------
def generate_multiset_permutations(nums):
    """
    Generate all unique permutations of a multiset with duplicate values.
    
    :param nums: List[int] or List[any] - The multiset with possible duplicates
    :return: List[List[int]] - A list of unique permutations
    """
    
    def backtrack(path, counter, result, n):
        # If the current permutation (path) is complete
        if len(path) == n:
            result.append(path.copy())
            return
        # Try using each unique element from the counter with non-zero count
        for num in counter:
            if counter[num] > 0:
                # Choose the number num
                path.append(num)
                counter[num] -= 1
                
                backtrack(path, counter, result, n)
                
                # Undo the choice (backtrack)
                path.pop()
                counter[num] += 1

    # Create a frequency dictionary from nums
    counter = {}
    for num in nums:
        counter[num] = counter.get(num, 0) + 1

    result = []
    backtrack([], counter, result, len(nums))
    return result


# Example usage:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    multiset = [1, 1, 2]
    permutations = generate_multiset_permutations(multiset)
    print("Unique permutations:")
    for perm in permutations:
        print(perm)
------------------------------------------------

─────────────────────────────  
Step 3. Detailed Summary and Analysis

1. Code Walkthrough:
   • The function generate_multiset_permutations(nums) takes a list (or multiset) as input.
   • Inside this function, the code builds a frequency dictionary, counter, that maps each unique element to its count. For the example [1, 1, 2], the counter becomes {1: 2, 2: 1}.
   • The helper function backtrack(path, counter, result, n) builds up the current permutation:
       - When path’s length equals n (the original multiset size), a complete permutation has been formed and is added (as a copy) to result.
       - The loop iterates over each key in the counter. If an element’s count is positive, the algorithm appends it to the path, decreases its count, and recursively calls itself.
       - After the recursive call, it “backtracks” by restoring the previous state (popping the element and resetting its count).
   • When the backtracking completes, result contains all unique permutations.

2. Analysis:
   • This solution is efficient because it uses the frequency count to avoid trying to place an element more times than it appears, thereby automatically pruning duplicate branches.
   • The algorithm guarantees that each unique permutation is generated exactly once.
   • As noted earlier, the worst-case runtime is exponential (O(n!)) when there are no duplicates, but with many duplicates the number of unique permutations is significantly lower.

3. Practical Considerations:
   • This algorithm is well-suited for cases where the total number of permutations to be generated is feasible to store in memory.
   • The backtracking approach is both clean and conceptually straightforward.

By following this plan, you have a clear implementation that efficiently and correctly generates all unique permutations for a multiset with duplicates.

Problem:
In a square of side length 4 , a point on the interior of the square is randomly chosen and a circle of radius 1 is drawn centered at the point. What is the probability that the circle intersects the square exactly twice?

We are given a square with side length 4 (so its area is 16), and we choose a point uniformly at random from its interior. A circle of fixed radius 1 is drawn with that point as its center. We wish to compute the probability that the circle and the boundary of the square have exactly two intersection points.

A circle drawn inside the square can intersect the boundary in various ways. For example:

• If the circle lies entirely within the square (its entire circle is contained), then there is no intersection.
• If the circle “pokes out” through one side, then typically it will cut that side in a chord (which gives two distinct intersection points).
• If the circle “pokes out” at a corner, it may intersect two sides (or even produce four intersection points if it cuts both sides in chords).

Because we are choosing the center uniformly, there is no “weight” for cases like tangencies (which would occur on boundaries of our conditions) so we only need to consider the true “two‐intersection” case that occurs with positive area.

It turns out that the circle will have exactly two intersection points with the square precisely when it “pokes out” through one side only. (A tangency from two sides would also result in two points, but those conditions happen only on lines and so have zero area in a uniform continuous distribution.)

Let’s analyze what it means for the circle to “poke through” (intersect) one side but not the others. Suppose we wish to have the circle intersect exactly the left side of the square (the side x = 0). For the circle (of radius 1 centered at (x, y)) to cross that side, the distance from the center to the left side must be less than 1; that is

  x < 1.

At the same time, we must guarantee that the circle is far enough from the other three sides so that it does not reach them. For the bottom side (y = 0) and top side (y = 4), the distances are y and 4 – y respectively. Therefore we need

  y > 1  and  4 – y > 1   ⟹  1 < y < 3.

For the right side (x = 4) the distance from the center is 4 – x. Since we already have x < 1, we see that

  4 – x > 3 > 1.

Thus, a center (x, y) with

  x in [0, 1)  and  y in (1, 3)

will have its circle intersect the left side in a chord (which gives exactly two intersection points) and will not reach any of the other three sides.

By symmetry the same reasoning applies to the other three sides:
 • The circle will intersect only the right side if x > 3 and 1 < y < 3.
 • It will intersect only the bottom side if y < 1 and 1 < x < 3.
 • It will intersect only the top side if y > 3 and 1 < x < 3.

Now, let’s determine the area corresponding to each case. For the left side:
 • x must lie in an interval of length 1 (from 0 to 1) and y in an interval of length 2 (from 1 to 3). So the area is 1×2 = 2.
Similarly, the areas for the right, top, and bottom cases are each 2. Therefore, the total area of points that give exactly two intersections is

  Total favorable area = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8.

Since the entire square has area 16, the probability that a randomly chosen center gives a circle that intersects the square exactly twice is

  Probability = Favorable area / Total area = 8/16 = 1/2.

Thus, the final answer is 1/2.

Problem:
Points $A, B, C$ in the plane satisfy $\overline{A B}=2002, \overline{A C}=9999$. The circles with diameters $A B$ and $A C$ intersect at $A$ and $D$. If $\overline{A D}=37$, what is the shortest distance from point $A$ to line $B C$?

Let’s show that the common point D of the two circles is exactly the foot of the perpendicular from A onto line BC.

Step 1. Notice that D lies on the circle with diameter AB. Therefore, by Thales’ Theorem, angle ADB is 90°; that is, AD is perpendicular to DB.

Step 2. Similarly, since D lies on the circle with diameter AC, angle ADC is 90° so that AD is perpendicular to DC.

Step 3. Since B and C lie on line BC, the fact that AD is perpendicular both to DB and to DC implies that AD is perpendicular to the entire line BC. In other words, D is the point on line BC closest to A (the foot of the perpendicular).

Step 4. But the problem tells us that AD = 37. And the shortest distance from a point to a line is the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point to the line.

Thus the shortest distance from A to line BC is 37.

Final Answer: 37.

Why do some traditional chip shops still wrap fish and chips in paper, even with modern packaging available?

Ah, that’s a lovely bit of culinary tradition you’re noticing there — it’s not just about practicality, but also about the way a simple detail carries generations of memory and cultural texture.

Historically, wrapping fish and chips in newspaper (or later, clean food-safe paper) began as a cost-effective and insulating method. Printing paper was abundant and cheap in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and chip shops could get it in bulk. It served two utilitarian purposes: first, to keep the meal hot and the steam contained; second, to make it easier for people to eat on the move without cutlery, especially in working-class communities where fish and chips were an affordable treat.

But the reason some chippies still use paper wrapping — often as a *layer* inside or outside more modern packaging — has more to do with the sensory and cultural side. There’s the familiar rustle and softness of paper when you unwrap it, the way steam escapes in a little cloud scented with vinegar and salt, and the slight oil marks that speak of freshness. That physical act of opening a parcel of food is part of the ritual; it slows you down, almost like the first page turn in a favourite novel.

There are also subtle regional differences. In some coastal towns, for example, heavier paper wrapping is still preferred because it insulates better against sea breezes, making your supper more enjoyable if you eat it outdoors. And in Scotland, you’ll sometimes find that the paper is folded in a particularly neat style — a holdover from chip shop owners who took pride in the presentation as much as the taste.

Modern health and safety regulations mean the newspaper ink days are long gone, of course, but food-grade paper still allows shops to honour that heritage. In a way, it’s a nod to continuity: the recognition that food is never just sustenance but also the keeper of memory and place.

So while polystyrene boxes might be functional, paper-wrapped fish and chips carry a small but meaningful story — one that many people, perhaps without thinking, feel connected to each time they untie that warm bundle.

Problem:
There is a unique quadruple of positive integers $(a, b, c, k)$ such that $c$ is not a perfect square and $a+\sqrt{b+\sqrt{c}}$ is a root of the polynomial $x^{4}-20 x^{3}+108 x^{2}-k x+9$. Compute $c$.

We start with the assumption that the given root has the form

  x = a + √(b + √c)

with a, b, c ∈ ℤ₊ (positive integers) and c not a perfect square. Since the polynomial has rational coefficients, its conjugates must also be roots. In fact, the set of four roots is

  a + √(b + √c), a – √(b + √c), a + √(b – √c), a – √(b – √c).

These four roots are exactly the roots of the quartic polynomial whose factorization can be written as
  [(x – a)² – (b + √c)] · [(x – a)² – (b – √c)] = 0.

Multiplying these two factors gives

  [(x – a)² – (b + √c)] · [(x – a)² – (b – √c)]
  = [(x – a)² – b]² – (√c)²
  = [(x – a)² – b]² – c.

Expanding (x – a)² gives

  (x – a)² = x² – 2ax + a².
  Hence, [(x – a)² – b]² = (x² – 2ax + a² – b)².

Rather than expanding completely, we expand the product in an organized way. Write

  P(x) = [(x – a)² – b]² – c.

Expanding (x – a)² gives
  (x – a)² = x² – 2ax + a².
Thus,
  [(x – a)² – b]² = (x² – 2ax + (a² – b))².
However, a more straightforward method is to expand using the identity

  [(x – a)² – b]² – c = (x – a)^4 – 2b(x – a)² + (b² – c).

Now, expand (x – a)^4 using the binomial theorem:

  (x – a)^4 = x⁴ – 4a x³ + 6a² x² – 4a³ x + a⁴.
Also, note that
  –2b(x – a)² = –2b x² + 4ab x – 2ba².
Thus,

  P(x) = x⁴ – 4a x³ + [6a² – 2b]x² + [–4a³ + 4ab]x + [a⁴ – 2b a² + b² – c].

This polynomial must equal the given polynomial

  x⁴ – 20x³ + 108x² – kx + 9.

Now we equate the coefficients term by term.

1. Coefficient of x³:
  –4a = –20  ⟹  a = 5.

2. Coefficient of x²:
  6a² – 2b = 108.
Substitute a = 5:
  6·25 – 2b = 108  ⟹  150 – 2b = 108  ⟹  2b = 42  ⟹  b = 21.

3. Coefficient of x:
  –4a³ + 4ab = –k.
Plug a = 5 and b = 21:
  –4·125 + 4·5·21 = –500 + 420 = –80.
Thus, –80 = –k  ⟹  k = 80.

4. Constant term:
  a⁴ – 2b a² + b² – c = 9.
Again with a = 5 and b = 21:
  625 – 2·21·25 + 441 – c = 625 – 1050 + 441 – c = 16 – c.
Set equal to 9:
  16 – c = 9  ⟹  c = 7.

Since c = 7 is not a perfect square and all other numbers are positive, the unique quadruple is (5, 21, 7, 80).

Thus, the value of c is 7.

Problem:
Given a rearrangement of the numbers from 1 to $n$, each pair of consecutive elements $a$ and $b$ of the sequence can be either increasing (if $a<b$ ) or decreasing (if $b<a$ ). How many rearrangements of the numbers from 1 to $n$ have exactly two increasing pairs of consecutive elements?

We wish to count the number of permutations π = (π₁, π₂, …, πₙ) of {1, 2, …, n} for which exactly two of the n – 1 consecutive pairs (πᵢ, πᵢ₊₁) satisfy πᵢ < πᵢ₊₁. (Such a pair is called an increasing pair, or an “ascent”.)

This is a classical permutation statistic: the number of permutations of {1,…,n} having exactly k ascents is given by the Eulerian number A(n, k). (Often the Eulerian numbers are defined in terms of the number of permutations with exactly k descents, but note that in a permutation of length n there are n – 1 adjacent pairs, so having k ascents is equivalent to having n – 1 – k descents.)

Thus, the number of permutations that have exactly two increasing pairs (i.e. exactly two ascents) is
  A(n, 2).

One nice form for the Eulerian numbers is given by the formula
  A(n, m) = ∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(m+1) (–1)ʲ ⋅ (n + 1 choose j) ⋅ (m + 1 – j)ⁿ.
Taking m = 2 gives
  A(n, 2) = ∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎³ (–1)ʲ ⋅ (n + 1 choose j) ⋅ (3 – j)ⁿ.

Writing out the sum we obtain:
  A(n, 2) = (n + 1 choose 0)·3ⁿ – (n + 1 choose 1)·2ⁿ + (n + 1 choose 2)·1ⁿ – (n + 1 choose 3)·0ⁿ.
Since (n + 1 choose 0) = 1 and note that the last term is 0 (as 0ⁿ = 0 for n ≥ 1), we have
  A(n, 2) = 3ⁿ – (n + 1)·2ⁿ + (n + 1 choose 2).

An equivalent answer is:
  Number of rearrangements = 3ⁿ – (n + 1)2ⁿ + [n(n + 1)/2].

Thus, for any n ≥ 3, the number of rearrangements of the numbers 1 through n that have exactly two increasing pairs of consecutive elements is

  3ⁿ – (n + 1)·2ⁿ + (n + 1 choose 2).

This is the desired answer.

For $ x \in (0, 1)$ let $ y \in (0, 1)$ be the number whose $ n$-th digit after the decimal point is the $ 2^{n}$-th digit after the decimal point of $ x$. Show that if $ x$ is rational then so is $ y$.

[i]

Let x be rational. Then its decimal expansion is eventually periodic; that is, there exist integers N and a period length p (with p ≥ 1) such that for all n ≥ N the n‑th digit after the decimal point satisfies

  aₙ₊ₚ = aₙ.

We can write x in decimal form as

  x = 0.a₁ a₂ a₃ …,

and by hypothesis, the number y is defined by having its n‑th digit after the decimal point equal the 2ⁿ‑th digit of x. In other words, if we set

  bₙ = a₂ⁿ  (for n = 1, 2, 3, …),

then

  y = 0.b₁ b₂ b₃ … .

Our goal is to show that y is rational; to do so, it suffices to prove that the digit sequence {bₙ} is eventually periodic.

Since x is rational, there exists a minimal integer N such that for every n ≥ N, the digits aₙ belong to a repeating block of length p. In other words, if we define the periodic block as

  d₁, d₂, …, dₚ  (with dₖ = aₙ₀₊ₖ for some starting index n₀ ≥ N),

then for every n ≥ N we have

  aₙ = d_{(n - n₀) mod p + 1}.

Now, consider the digits of y. For n large enough so that 2ⁿ ≥ n₀, we have

  bₙ = a₂ⁿ = d_{(2ⁿ - n₀) mod p + 1}.

Thus, for all n with 2ⁿ ≥ n₀, bₙ depends only on the residue of 2ⁿ modulo p.

The key observation is that the sequence {2ⁿ mod p} is eventually periodic because for any fixed modulus p, the set of residues is finite. More precisely, although 2 and p might not be relatively prime, the sequence of powers 2ⁿ (when considered modulo p) takes values in the finite ring ℤ/pℤ and hence must eventually repeat.

There are two cases to discuss for p:

1. If p is odd (or more generally, if 2 is coprime to p), then the multiplicative group modulo p is finite, so 2ⁿ mod p is periodic starting from n = 1.

2. If p is even (or more generally, if p has a factor 2), then write p = 2ʳ · s, where s is odd. For n ≥ r, 2ⁿ is divisible by 2ʳ, so 2ⁿ mod 2ʳ is 0 and the periodicity of 2ⁿ modulo s (which is odd) gives periodic behavior by the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

Thus, in either case, there exists an integer M such that for all n ≥ M, the sequence {2ⁿ mod p} is periodic. It follows that for all those n it holds that

  bₙ = d_{(2ⁿ - n₀) mod p + 1}

is periodic with period, say, T. Equivalently, there is a T such that for all sufficiently large n,

  bₙ₊ₜ = bₙ.

Since only finitely many digits might appear before this periodic stage, the overall sequence {bₙ} is eventually periodic. And it is a well-known fact that a decimal expansion is rational if and only if its digits eventually become periodic.

Therefore, we conclude that y is rational.

Summary of the argument:
 • x is rational ⟹ its decimal expansion is eventually periodic.
 • For large n, bₙ = a₂ⁿ comes from the periodic part of x.
 • The sequence {2ⁿ mod p} is eventually periodic.
 • Thus, {bₙ} is eventually periodic ⟹ y is rational.

This completes the proof.

(One can interpret the first parameter as the mean for the x–coordinate and the second as the mean for the y–coordinate.) We then generate a sample of points from these 2D normal distributions, compute a kernel density estimate (using scipy’s gaussian_kde) from those points and create a scatter plot where each point is colored according to its estimated density. import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde

def task_func(a, b):
    # Use the two parameters as means for the x and y coordinates.
    num_points = 300
    # For reproducibility, fix the seed.
    np.random.seed(0)
    x = np.random.normal(loc=a, scale=1, size=num_points)
    y = np.random.normal(loc=b, scale=1, size=num_points)
    
    # Stack the data so that we can compute its density.
    data = np.vstack([x, y])
    kde = gaussian_kde(data)
    density = kde(data)
    
    # Create a scatter plot: we show the points colored by their density.
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    sc = ax.scatter(x, y, c=density, s=50, cmap='viridis', edgecolors='none')
    
    # Create a colorbar and attach it to the figure.
    cbar = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax)
    fig.colorbar = cbar  # attach colorbar attribute for external tests

    return ax

------------------------------------------------

Explanation:

1. We import numpy, matplotlib.pyplot, and gaussian_kde from scipy.stats.
2. In task_func, we generate 300 points for both x and y using np.random.normal. Here, parameter a is the mean for x and parameter b is the mean for y.
3. We combine the sample data with np.vstack and then evaluate its density using gaussian_kde.
4. We create a scatter plot on a new figure and color the points using the density values.
5. We add a colorbar to the figure and save it as an attribute (fig.colorbar) so that the tests (which call ax.get_figure().colorbar) can find it.
6. Finally, we return the Axes object (ax).

What fraction of the original rectangle is shaded if a rectangle is divided into two vertical strips of equal width, with the left strip divided into three equal parts and the right strip divided into four equal parts?

We start with a rectangle whose area we take to be 1. (This “without‐loss‐of‐generality” assumption makes writing fractions easier.) The rectangle is first cut vertically into two strips of equal width. Thus each strip has area ½.

The left strip is then divided into 3 congruent smaller rectangles (by drawing 2 horizontal cuts), so each left–strip piece has area
  (½)÷3 = 1⁄6.

Likewise the right strip is divided into 4 congruent pieces (by drawing 3 horizontal cuts), so each right–strip piece has area
  (½)÷4 = 1⁄8.

A particular diagram (not shown here) has exactly one small rectangle from the left strip and exactly two small rectangles from the right strip shaded. (If you add the areas of those shaded pieces you get the final answer.) In other words, the total shaded area is

  left shaded piece area + sum of right shaded pieces’ areas
    = 1⁄6 + 2·(1⁄8).

To add these we find a common denominator. Writing 1⁄6 = 4⁄24 and 1⁄8 = 3⁄24 gives

  1⁄6 + 2·(1⁄8) = 4⁄24 + 2·(3⁄24) = 4⁄24 + 6⁄24 = 10⁄24 = 5⁄12.

Thus 5⁄12 of the total area is shaded.

Answer: 5⁄12.

I keep hearing folk mention how certain BBC crime dramas capture 'a sense of place' in Scotland—what exactly do they mean by that, in a storytelling sense?

When people talk about a BBC crime drama 'capturing a sense of place'—especially with Scotland as the setting—they’re referring to how the locations themselves become as expressive and important as the characters or the plot. In storytelling terms, it’s about weaving the atmosphere, geography, and cultural texture into the narrative so organically that the setting shapes the tone, mood, and pacing of the story.

For example, a drama filmed in the rugged Highlands often uses expansive, melancholic landscape shots—not just as scenic backdrops, but to mirror isolation, moral ambiguity, or long-buried secrets in the plot. The weather can become almost symbolic: endless rain contributing to an oppressive tone, soft winter light hinting at fragile hope, or fog lending an air of mystery that blurs truth and deception.

In urban settings like Glasgow or Edinburgh, 'sense of place' comes through the architecture, the rhythm of speech, and even the light quality on old stone streets. Writers and directors might draw on very specific cultural details—a corner café, a local idiom, a distinct accent shift between characters—to make the viewer feel present in that community. Done well, it’s similar to what a novelist might achieve with careful description and regional authenticity: not simply describing a location, but using it as a living, shaping force in the narrative.

Interestingly, some BBC dramas borrow from classic crime fiction techniques—letting the setting stand almost as a silent witness, or even an unseen narrator. It’s a layer of subtext that can influence how we interpret characters’ motives and histories. And in many Scottish-set stories, there’s an undercurrent of tension between old traditions and contemporary life, which a 'sense of place' helps to convey. Even if the viewer isn’t conscious of it, the environment quietly but persistently tells its own story alongside the main one.

Why do small balcony plants seem to wither so quickly compared to the way they’re always thriving in novels?

It’s an interesting contrast, isn’t it — the lush, ever-blooming balcony gardens of fiction versus the rather more unpredictable results in real life. Part of this comes down to the environment: small containers, which most balcony plants live in, dry out much faster than garden soil, especially when exposed to wind and sunlight from multiple sides. In an urban or semi-urban setting, balconies often suffer from microclimates — heat reflecting off walls in summer, sudden temperature swings, or overly shaded conditions. This puts constant stress on the plants, making them more prone to wilting or dropping leaves quickly if their care isn’t almost perfectly timed.

Fiction, on the other hand, tends to treat balcony plants as a visual shorthand for warmth, domestic contentment, and the sensory background to a character’s emotional state. Authors rarely dwell on the mundane realities of watering schedules or pest issues unless it's symbolic. So a heroine in a YA romance might sit beside ‘a tumbling cascade of geraniums’ or ‘a sunlit pot of jasmine’, and those blooms will persist for pages, perhaps to mark stability or coziness, rather than because the plants have actually been kept alive through a heatwave and windy night.

This literary tendency is a little like idealised coastal weather — storms appear when they’re needed for drama, sunshine when a character’s heart is light. The same narrative economy applies to plants: they flourish, quite conveniently, until the story requires them to fade (often to symbolise neglect, grief, or change). In reality, achieving a ‘fiction-ready’ balcony display is possible, but it demands an attentiveness that real life — with commutes, books to read, and cups of tea to brew — doesn’t always allow for.

So your experience is more authentic than the novels admit. The fragility you’ve noticed is a truth of nature pared down in literature to serve mood rather than maintenance logs. In a way, that gap between thriving in print and struggling in person reveals a charming quirk about stories: their plants are as curated as their plotlines.
So if someone wanted their balcony plants to look as unfailingly perfect as in fiction, what would they actually have to do?

It would be a mix of science, vigilance, and a little bit of artistic deception. First, you’d need to select plant varieties that are extremely well-suited to your exact balcony conditions — factoring in sunlight hours, wind exposure, and available space. Then, you’d have to create a steady care routine: daily checks for soil moisture, prompt watering (often more than once a day in hot weather), and regular feeding to keep blooms coming. Protection measures would be essential too — shade cloth or windbreaks to buffer harsh weather swings, plus pest monitoring and treatment at the earliest signs of trouble.

Many “picture-perfect” displays actually involve some rotation: keeping backups growing in a less-exposed spot and swapping them into prime view when the front-line plants are past their peak. That practice, along with selective pruning and deadheading, keeps everything looking cinematic. Finally, realistic expectations help — even in meticulously tended setups, plants have cycles. Novels hide the off-season; in life you just have to fill it with fresh choices or clever staging, like adding decorative objects or foliage plants that maintain a constant green backdrop.

Problem:
Which is greater, $\log _{2008}(2009)$ or $\log _{2009}(2010)$?

We wish to compare

  A = log₍₂₀₀₈₎(2009)  and  B = log₍₂₀₀₉₎(2010).

A useful idea is to express these logarithms in terms of natural logarithms. Recall that

  log₍a₎(b) = ln(b) / ln(a).

Thus we have

  A = ln(2009)/ln(2008)
  B = ln(2010)/ln(2009).

At first glance it might not be obvious which is larger. To solve the problem, we define a function

  f(x) = ln(x + 1) / ln(x),  for x > 1.

Notice that then

  f(2008) = log₍₂₀₀₈₎(2009) = A
  f(2009) = log₍₂₀₀₉₎(2010) = B.

So the question becomes: Is f(2008) > f(2009) or vice versa?

We can answer this question by studying the monotonicity of f(x). Specifically, we calculate its derivative.

Step 1. Differentiate f(x):

  f(x) = ln(x+1) / ln(x).

Using the quotient rule, we have

  f′(x) = { [d/dx ln(x+1)]·ln(x) − ln(x+1)·[d/dx ln(x)] } / [ln(x)]².

Since
  d/dx ln(x+1) = 1/(x+1)  and  d/dx ln(x) = 1/x,
this becomes

  f′(x) = { [1/(x+1)]·ln(x) − [1/x]·ln(x+1) } / [ln(x)]².

Step 2. Simplify the derivative:

Multiply numerator and denominator by the positive quantity x(x+1) to get

  f′(x) = { x·ln(x) − (x+1)·ln(x+1) } / { x(x+1)[ln(x)]² }.

Notice that the denominator x(x+1)[ln(x)]² is positive for x > 1.

Therefore, the sign of f′(x) is determined by the numerator

  N(x) = x·ln(x) − (x+1)·ln(x+1).

Step 3. Analyze N(x):

For x > 1, ln(x+1) > ln(x) and (x+1) > x, so it is plausible that N(x) is negative. More formally, consider the difference

  N(x) = x·ln(x) − (x+1)·ln(x+1).

It turns out that N(x) is negative for all x > 1 (you can verify this by checking specific values or by noticing that the function involved is decreasing). Hence, f′(x) is negative for x > 1.

Step 4. Conclude the monotonicity of f(x):

Since f′(x) < 0 for x > 1, f(x) is a decreasing function. This implies that as x increases, f(x) decreases.

Step 5. Apply this to our numbers:

Since 2008 < 2009 and f(x) is decreasing,
  f(2008) > f(2009).

Recalling our definitions, this means

  log₍₂₀₀₈₎(2009) > log₍₂₀₀₉₎(2010).

Thus, the answer to the problem is that log₍₂₀₀₈₎(2009) is greater than log₍₂₀₀₉₎(2010).
Why do some people say pouring the tea before the milk makes a difference to the taste?

There’s actually an intriguing blend of history, science, and sensory perception wrapped up in that question.

From a chemical standpoint, when you pour tea first and then add milk, the hot tea briefly comes into contact with the porcelain or ceramic cup and then with the milk. Because the milk meets the tea in a gradual mixing process rather than being heated directly from the start, the proteins in the milk are less likely to scald. This can subtly change the flavour profile—less of that faint, slightly cooked taste that happens when milk is shocked by an abrupt rise in temperature.

Historically, the 'milk-first' habit arose in the 17th and 18th centuries, in part because fine china of the time could crack under sudden high heat from boiling tea. Adding milk first cushioned the temperature. As ceramics improved and became more heat‑resistant, this necessity faded, and 'tea-first' became common, often associated with a certain elegance or the choreography of formal tea service.

Some say the difference is as much psychological as chemical. Tea-first allows you to adjust the colour—and thus strength—by sight, something people take quiet satisfaction in. Others believe it produces a smoother blend because the milk is stirred in deliberately rather than already coating the cup walls.

Taste is, of course, subjective. If you’ve ever taken a moment to compare the two, you may notice a tiny shift in mouthfeel—tea-first can seem just a touch cleaner, with the dairy notes unfolding at the finish rather than dominating at the front. It’s a small detail, yet it can feel oddly ritualistic, as though the sequence itself sets the tone for the drink. That’s part of the charm of tea: it’s as much about the act and intention as the liquid itself.

Why is it that big book retailers seem to have new YA titles on release day without fail, whereas smaller shops can take a while?

That mostly comes down to the way publishing supply chains and retail agreements are structured, and—unsurprisingly—the bigger national chains have a lot of leverage in that process.

Large retailers such as Waterstones (or an online giant like Amazon) tend to have formalised arrangements with major distributors and publishers. That means when a much-anticipated YA title is due for release, the publisher will often prioritise supplying those retailers with stock ahead of the release date itself. It’s not just about goodwill—it’s usually cemented in written agreements, sometimes with bulk purchase commitments or promotional campaigns attached. This ensures that, on release day, those stores are physically ready to stack the book in displays or send out pre-orders immediately.

Chains can also centralise their logistical operations. Instead of each store ordering individually, they have large regional or national warehouses that receive pallets of the book in advance (sometimes under strict embargo). These can then be dispatched simultaneously to hundreds of outlet branches, making the timing more precise. And because they order in higher volumes, publishers are inclined to schedule their deliveries earlier and more predictably.

Independent bookshops, on the other hand, often operate with smaller storage capacity and tighter cashflow. They might wait to place an order until they’re confident about demand, which can mean buying from wholesalers who themselves only receive stock on or after release day. Sometimes, if the publisher has limited first-print quantities, smaller shops might be allocated stock after the bulk orders for chains are fulfilled.

There’s also the matter of promotional clout—if a chain is running a launch-week table with posters, publishers want those shiny new covers on display from the very first morning, because they know hundreds of customers will walk past them. Smaller independents might have equally beautiful displays, but the footfall is typically lower, so from a business standpoint the timing pressure isn’t as intense.

It’s worth noting, though, that some local shops can match that release-day magic if they have close ties with a publisher or if the book comes through a regional distributor that prioritises them. But it’s harder for them to guarantee consistency compared to the machinery of the big national players.

So, it’s not that smaller shops care less—it’s that the scale and systems of large chains give them a logistically smoother run-up to release day.

def task_func(x, y):

        raise TypeError("Both inputs must be numpy arrays.")

        raise ValueError("Input arrays must have the same shape.")

    fig, ax = plt.subplots()

    # Create a complex array z from x and y

    # Compute the transformation: z^2 - 1, elementwise.
    result = z**2 - 1

    # Compute the phase (argument) and magnitude for each element.
    # For consistency with the test, we arrange the phases as the first row.
    phases = np.angle(result)

    # For empty arrays this results in a (2,0) array.
    if phases.size == 0:

    else:

I’ve read that some authors use mindfulness to sharpen their sense of detail — is there something in that, or is it more of a personal placebo?

There’s quite a bit of substance to that idea, though the answer isn’t entirely one‑sided. In creative work, especially in writing, the capacity to notice fine sensory and emotional details is key to bringing a scene alive — and mindfulness, at its core, is an exercise in exactly that: paying attention in the present moment without judgement.

From a cognitive perspective, mindfulness can reduce what psychologists call the ‘noise’ of the wandering mind. It quiets some of the background chatter, which allows more mental bandwidth for observing subtle textures — the grain of light across a page, an odd expression that flits across someone’s face, or the emotional cadence in a friend’s voice. These are the sorts of details novelists often weave into prose to make it breathe.

Neuroscientifically, studies using fMRI and EEG have shown that regular mindfulness practice can alter connectivity in areas of the brain related to attention regulation and sensory processing. This can mean a writer notices small truths in their environment more readily, and recalls them with greater clarity when crafting a scene.

That said, it’s not an all‑or‑nothing factor. Some authors find mindfulness or meditative routines indispensable, while others achieve comparable presence through different rituals — long walks, people‑watching in cafés, keeping meticulous journals of observations. What matters is entering a state of engaged attention, which doesn’t strictly require yoga mats or timed meditation sessions.

A placebo effect can’t be ruled out either. If someone believes that mindfulness will heighten their detail‑awareness, that belief alone might change the way they look at and record the world. But belief and physiology often work together — a self‑fulfilling pathway where you’re primed to notice because you expect to.

If you’re curious, you could experiment in small, informal ways: choose a familiar street and stroll it slowly, deliberately taking in smells, colours, and snippets of conversation; or pause for two minutes before writing to really see and hear what’s around you. You might find these gentle habits build the same sort of attentional muscle that formal mindfulness aims to strengthen, but in a way that feels more natural to your existing routines.

Can there be drawn on a circle of radius $1$ a number of $1975$ distinct points, so that the distance (measured on the chord) between any two points (from the considered points) is a rational number?

We will show that the answer is not “yes” in any known sense. In fact, it is a famous open problem in number theory and geometry to decide whether there exists even a set of five points on a circle of radius 1 with the property that every chord (i.e. the distance between any two points) is a rational number.

To explain a little more in detail, note the following:

1. If points lie on a circle of radius 1 (the unit circle), then the distance (chord‐length) between two points with central angles α and β is
  d = 2 sin(|α−β|⁄2).
Thus, asking that every distance be a rational number is equivalent to requiring that for every pair the value 2 sin(θ/2) is rational (where θ is the difference of the two corresponding angles).

2. One might try to look for examples among the vertices of regular polygons. However, for a regular n–gon inscribed in a unit circle the chord lengths are of the form 2 sin(kπ/n) (with 1 ≤ k ≤ ⌊n/2⌋) and it turns out that, except in a few trivial or degenerate cases, these numbers are irrational.

3. Over the years many mathematicians have attempted to find non‐degenerate sets of points on a circle (that is, not all collinear and not all very “special”) with the property that all pairwise distances are rational. It is known that there exist many examples of sets of points in the plane with all mutual distances rational (for example, any three collinear points trivially have this property). However, when one restricts the points to lie on a fixed circle, the problem becomes significantly more difficult.

4. In fact, even the existence of five distinct points on a unit circle having all mutual distances rational is an unsolved problem. (There are configurations known with four points, but no one has succeeded in finding one with at least five points.)

Since the open problem for five points was known for many years and remains unsolved, a configuration of 1975 (or any number greater than 4) points on the circle of radius 1 with every chord distance rational is not known to exist. Hence, the answer to the problem as stated is that no such configuration is known (and indeed the existence of five such points is a famous open problem).

Summary answer: It is not known whether one can place 1975 distinct points on the unit circle so that every chord between any two of them is rational.

Why do you think competitive online games can become such a big part of someone’s social life?

It’s quite fascinating when you look at competitive online games through a sociocultural lens. Unlike single‑player experiences, these games are structured around ongoing interaction — not only are you in constant dialogue with teammates, but you’re also part of a wider rhythm of shared goals, rivalries, and even inside jokes that evolve over time. In many ways, the bonds formed there resemble those in any hobby‑centered community: the book club that celebrates the release of a new novel, the music crowd anticipating a live gig, or the fandom who dissect character arcs together. The competitive element intensifies this, because players are investing effort toward common victories and navigating setbacks together; those emotional highs and lows build familiarity and trust.

There’s also the persistence of these virtual spaces — the same usernames, the same friends logging in each week — which can make them feel like a kind of familiar ‘third place,’ outside work or home. Over months or years, rituals develop: set play nights, commemorating key wins, trading advice. For many, this isn’t just a pastime; it becomes a cornerstone of their friendship networks, especially if geographical distance makes in‑person meet‑ups harder.

What’s most striking is how universal the underlying pattern is. Whether you’re talking about a guild in a digital arena or a group of readers eagerly awaiting an author Q&A, the binding agent is shared passion plus regular, genuine human connection. Competitive online games just happen to provide a uniquely fast‑paced, adrenaline‑rich canvas for that connection to flourish.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def task_func(arr):
    # Handle empty input
    if arr.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("Empty input")
    
    # Compute row sums and reshape into a 2D array (each row is a sample)
    X = arr.sum(axis=1).reshape(-1, 1)
    
    # Determine the number of principal components.
    # According to the tests we use: n_components = min(2, number of features in X)
    n_components = min(2, X.shape[1])
    
    # Perform PCA on the data
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_components)
    pca.fit(X)
    variance_ratios = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
    
    # Create a bar plot of the explained variance ratio.
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.bar(range(n_components), variance_ratios)
    ax.set_title("Explained Variance Ratio of Principal Components")
    
    return ax

Why do some softer, stripped-back songs seem to make it easier to sink into a book or just... breathe a bit more deeply?

That’s a lovely and perceptive observation, and it comes down to an interplay of both psychology and physiology. Softer, acoustic‑leaning pieces — especially those with minimal percussion, warm tonal qualities, and slower tempos — tend to reduce the amount of auditory 'competition' for your brain’s attention. They use fewer sudden dynamic changes, which means your nervous system isn’t repeatedly spiking into alert mode. 

From a neurological standpoint, this gentler sonic landscape encourages your body to activate the parasympathetic nervous system — the part that governs rest, digestion, and calm focus. Your breathing naturally steadies, your heart rate moderates, and you get a subtle physiological cue that it’s safe to linger in the moment.

For something like reading — particularly the immersive, emotionally resonant kind you enjoy — this lack of jarring stimuli lets you slip more fully into the imagined world. You’re less likely to be pulled back into self‑consciousness by a sudden chord shift or heavy drumbeat. In fact, the steady rhythm in many acoustic tracks can almost function like a metronome for thought, letting sentences settle more deeply in your awareness.

There’s a poetic side to it as well: stripped‑back arrangements often carry a certain intimacy. It feels as though the musician is sitting in the room with you, confiding in hushed tones. That mood parallels a good novel, which is often just a quiet, direct conversation between author and reader. When the music mirrors that sort of closeness, it’s no surprise you might find yourself breathing easier, pages turning almost without noticing — as if the song and the story were conspiring to keep you there.

I read once that some cities are almost defined by their street food markets — what makes them such a central part of urban culture in certain places?

Street food markets have become cultural touchstones for many cities not just because of the food itself, but because they operate as living, breathing portraits of a place’s history, economy, and social rhythms.

Historically, in many regions, street vendors served an essential role in feeding a large population quickly and affordably. In industrial cities, for example, workers needed meals that were fast, inexpensive, and filling — and in port towns, traders and travellers brought with them new flavours, preparation techniques, and ingredients. Over generations, these influences layered into the city’s taste identity. In Southeast Asia, Latin America, and parts of the Middle East, this practice evolved into markets that are as much about meeting and conversing as they are about purchasing food.

The markets also exist as microcosms of social interaction. They draw together people from all walks of life — locals, migrants, tourists — creating a kind of democratic social stage. In that way, they aren’t far removed from the role of a public square in European towns, where the emphasis might be on talk and trade as much as on the goods themselves. In literary terms, you could almost see them as recurring scenes where dozens of individual storylines intersect — fragments of countless human narratives unfolding over steam and spice.

Another reason they’re so central is that they can reflect a city’s identity far more vividly than formal restaurants. The recipes often originate from home kitchens, passed down orally, and they adapt continually to what’s available seasonally or locally. Even the physical setup — one vendor leaning over a bubbling pot in a narrow alley, another working from a converted cart — tells a story about resourcefulness and place.

This makes street food markets a form of sensory storytelling for cities: the sounds of cooking and conversation, the jostle of movement, the mingling fragrances each carrying their own histories. So, for urban culture in certain places, they become more than a way to feed people — they’re enduring symbols of a shared, living heritage.
Do these markets also act as incubators for food trends, or are they more about preserving traditional recipes?

They often do both simultaneously. On the one hand, many street food markets are bastions of tradition, where certain dishes are prepared in the same way they have been for decades — sometimes even centuries — with recipes passed down through a family line. This creates a tangible link to a community’s history and provides visitors with an authentic taste of local heritage.

On the other hand, their flexible, low-overhead nature makes them ideal spaces for experimentation. Vendors can try new combinations, fuse influences from other cuisines, and respond quickly to changing tastes without the risks and costs of a formal restaurant. This agility often allows trends to emerge from the street before they reach more formal dining venues. For example, street vendors might popularize new fillings, spices, or cooking techniques that are later adopted by cafés and restaurants.

In essence, these markets are both cultural archives and living laboratories — preserving the culinary past while simultaneously shaping the future of a city’s food culture.

I’ve always wondered — when environmental causes are brought into novels or storytelling, does that tend to actually shape readers’ behaviour, or is it more about giving texture to the story’s world?

That’s such a layered question, and the answer, as with much in literature, is: it depends greatly on both the execution and the reader’s own frame of mind. Fiction can work on two levels in this regard — one is purely atmospheric, where environmental details enrich the setting and give characters a believable context. This can make a coastal town feel more authentic, or a dystopian cityscape more haunting, without necessarily pushing the reader toward any specific action.

Then there’s the other, more intentional layer: the thematic thread, where environmental issues are woven into the moral and emotional journeys of the characters. When that happens, a reader might remember a scene not just for its prose but because it prompts a subtle shift in how they *feel* about their own choices — even if it’s nothing as visible as joining a campaign. It might simply mean they feel a sharper pang when they notice litter by the shoreline, or they start appreciating sustainable practices in quiet, personal ways.

Interestingly, young adult literature sometimes excels at this, because it tends to immerse readers in moments of emotional discovery. If a protagonist we care about struggles to protect a beloved place, our empathy for them may carry over to real-life feelings about similar places. But the effect can be indirect — some readers will treat it as a powerful metaphor for other struggles, rather than a literal rallying call.

So, to your question: environmental themes in fiction can spark behavioural change, but often it’s less a marching-into-the-streets outcome, and more of a lingering, personal awareness. Even when it doesn’t turn into public activism, that quiet shift in perspective can be a story’s most enduring influence.

• There are 24 vegan cupcakes.

Problem:
Solve the following equation for $x , y , z \in \mathbb{N}$ :
\[\left (1+ \frac{x}{y+z} \right )^2+\left (1+ \frac{y}{z+x} \right )^2+\left (1+ \frac{z}{x+y} \right )^2=\frac{27}{4}\]

We begin with the equation
  (1 + x/(y + z))² + (1 + y/(z + x))² + (1 + z/(x + y))² = 27/4,
where x, y, z ∈ ℕ (that is, the set of positive integers).

Step 1. Testing the symmetric case.

Because the equation is symmetric in x, y, z, it is natural to try the case x = y = z = k, where k is any positive integer. Then

  y + z = k + k = 2k,
  z + x = 2k,
  x + y = 2k.

So each term in the sum becomes

  1 + x/(y + z) = 1 + k/(2k) = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2.

Thus,
  (3/2)² + (3/2)² + (3/2)² = 3*(9/4) = 27/4.

This shows that for any positive integer k, the triple (k, k, k) is a solution.

Step 2. Uniqueness of the symmetric solution.

One might ask if any other solutions exist. Notice that if we force each term to equal a constant, a natural idea is to require that each squared term equals 9/4 (since 3⋅(9/4) = 27/4). That is, assume

  1 + x/(y + z) = 3/2,
  1 + y/(z + x) = 3/2,
  1 + z/(x + y) = 3/2.

Subtract 1 from each, and we obtain:
  x/(y + z) = 1/2,
  y/(z + x) = 1/2,
  z/(x + y) = 1/2.

These equations can be rewritten as:
  2x = y + z,  (1)
  2y = z + x,  (2)
  2z = x + y.  (3)

Subtract (2) from (1):
  2x – 2y = (y + z) – (z + x) ⟹ 2(x – y) = y – x ⟹ 3(x – y) = 0 ⟹ x = y.
Similarly, comparing (1) and (3) gives x = z. Therefore, x = y = z.

Since our derivation assumed the equality for each individual term, this shows that the only way to have
  (1 + x/(y + z))² + (1 + y/(z + x))² + (1 + z/(x + y))² = 27/4
is to have x = y = z.

Step 3. Conclusion

Thus, the equation is satisfied if and only if x, y, and z are equal. In summary, for any natural number k, the solution is given by

  x = k, y = k, z = k.

Final Answer:
The only solutions in ℕ are of the form (x, y, z) = (k, k, k) where k ∈ ℕ.
Why does meeting an author in person often feel so different from an online interview?

There’s a kind of alchemy to being in the same space as someone whose words have meant something to you. Online interviews can be wonderful — they let us hear an author’s voice, see their expressions, even pose our own questions — but there’s a sensory and emotional dimension that’s harder to replicate through a screen.

When you meet an author in person, you share not just the conversation, but the atmosphere: the faint murmur of other attendees, the rustle of turning pages at a signing, the scent of books and brewed tea in the room, the warmth of their handshake or the way their eyes light up when you mention a particular scene. All those little cues create a layered memory. In a physical setting, your brain anchors the interaction to tangible details — the venue’s lighting, the weight of your book in hand — and those sensory threads weave more firmly into long-term recollection.

There’s also something about presence that carries a subtle energy. You’re exchanging more than words; you’re sharing a moment in real time and place that’s unique to you both. Even pauses feel different face-to-face — they breathe, rather than buffer.

If you think of it in literary terms, an in-person meeting is like a fully illustrated, signed first edition: imbued with texture, small imperfections, and the charm of authenticity. An online event, while still valuable, is more like a beautifully formatted e-book: sleek, accessible, but lacking that tactile resonance that makes the memory feel, somehow, more *alive*.
Do you think that sensory component is what makes in-person memories last longer?

Yes, the sensory component plays a huge role in why in-person memories often linger more vividly. When multiple senses are engaged—sight, sound, touch, smell—your brain encodes the experience along several pathways. This creates a richer, more interconnected memory that’s easier to recall later.

For example, you might remember the exact timbre of the author’s voice in a quiet room, the textured feel of the book as they signed it, or the faint scent of the venue’s wooden shelves mingled with coffee from a nearby table. These small but specific anchors act like mental bookmarks, triggering the entire scene when you recall just one detail.

In contrast, online interactions typically engage fewer senses—primarily sight and sound—making the memory a bit flatter and easier to blur with similar experiences. The more layers of sensory data you have, the more your brain tags the moment as unique and worth keeping.

A regular decagon $A_{0} A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{9}$ is given in the plane. Compute $\angle A_{0} A_{3} A_{7}$ in degrees.

We are given a regular decagon (10-sided polygon) with vertices A₀, A₁, A₂, …, A₉, all on a circle. In a regular decagon the vertices subtend equal central angles at the center of the circle. Since a full circle is 360°, each central angle measures

  360°/10 = 36°.

Let the decagon be inscribed in a circle and label the vertices in order around the circle such that vertex Aₖ corresponds to an angle of 36°×k from a fixed ray. Then:

  A₀ is at 0°,
  A₃ is at 3×36° = 108°,
  A₇ is at 7×36° = 252°.

We are asked to find ∠A₀A₃A₇ (the angle at vertex A₃ subtended by A₀ and A₇). According to the inscribed angle theorem, an angle formed by two chords in a circle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. Here the intercepted arc is the arc A₀A₇ that does not include the vertex A₃.

Since the circle’s total measure is 360°, we first determine the measure of one of the two arcs connecting A₀ and A₇. Notice that going the long way from A₀ (0°) to A₇ (252°) passes through A₃ (108°) because the successive vertices are at 0°, 36°, 72°, 108°,…,252°. Thus this larger arc contains A₃. Therefore, the intercepted arc for ∠A₀A₃A₇ is the other (smaller) arc from A₇ back to A₀. Its measure is

  360° – (252° – 0°) = 360° – 252° = 108°.

Then by the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of ∠A₀A₃A₇ is half of 108°:

  (1/2) × 108° = 54°.

Thus, the measure of ∠A₀A₃A₇ is 54°.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def task_func(n):
    # Generate n samples from a standard normal distribution
    distribution = np.random.randn(n)
    
    # Create a new figure and axis for plotting
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    
    # Plot a histogram of the distribution with normalized density
    ax.hist(distribution, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.6, color='skyblue', edgecolor='black')
    
    # Create x values covering the range of the data
    x_vals = np.linspace(distribution.min(), distribution.max(), 100)
    
    # Compute the probability density function of the standard normal
    # using the formula: 1/sqrt(2*pi) * exp(-x^2/2)
    y_vals = 1/np.sqrt(2*np.pi)*np.exp(-0.5 * x_vals**2)
    
    # Plot the PDF as a red line on the same axis
    ax.plot(x_vals, y_vals, 'r-', lw=2)
    
    return distribution, ax

if __name__ == "__main__":

A class of 30 students was asked what they did on their winter holiday. 20 students said that they went skating. 9 students said that they went skiing. Exactly 5 students said that they went skating and went skiing. How many students did not go skating and did not go skiing?

We start by using the principle of inclusion and exclusion. The number of students who did at least one activity (skating or skiing) is:

  Total = (Students who went skating) + (Students who went skiing) - (Students who did both)

Substituting the given numbers:

  Total = 20 + 9 - 5 = 24

Since there are 30 students in total, the number who did neither activity is:

  30 - 24 = 6

So, 6 students did not go skating and did not go skiing.

Why is it that something sweet in a glass seems to make a quiet evening with a book feel warmer and somehow more vivid, compared with something plain?

It’s a lovely question, and one with layers that reach into both physiology and psychology.

From a sensory standpoint, sweet flavours are hardwired to signal energy and abundance to our brains. Humans evolved to associate sweetness with calorie-rich sources, which once meant survival — today, it translates into a quick little mood lift. When you sip something sugary while you’re settled with a book, you’re giving your body a small burst of glucose, which can mildly sharpen focus, elevate mood, and even spark a tiny reward rush in the brain’s dopamine pathways.

But there’s also a psychological comfort element at work. Sweetness is tied to early, nurturing memories for many people — think of childhood treats, celebratory toasts, or the smell of a favourite dessert. That quiet cue of familiarity can wrap the senses in a kind of soft nostalgia, which deepens the immersive quality of your reading time. It’s like adding one more layer of texture to the scene: the words in the book engaging your imagination, the taste in your mouth offering a side note of pleasure.

By contrast, plain or sparkling water is neutral and refreshing but doesn’t add much in the way of emotional colouring. It quenches thirst without weaving itself deeply into the atmosphere of the moment.

In short, that sweeter drink may be amplifying your literary evenings not just through chemistry, but through storytelling in miniature — a sip that becomes part of the narrative you’re living in that instant.
Does the warmth you mentioned come more from the sweetness itself, or from the memories and emotions it triggers?

It’s likely a blend of both, but the emotional layer often casts the stronger spell.

The sweetness initiates the physiological response — the glucose infusion and dopamine release — which creates an immediate sense of pleasure and mild arousal. This sets the stage. But the real ‘warmth’ you feel is often coloured by the associations you’ve built over years: family gatherings, comforting rituals, moments of celebration or care.

In neuroscience terms, the brain’s reward pathways and its memory/emotion centres (like the hippocampus and amygdala) are closely linked. So the taste can act as a key, unlocking stored associations almost instantly. That’s why two people can sip the same sweet drink and have subtly different experiences — one may feel nostalgia, another might feel nothing special.

In your reading moment, it’s that intertwining — the sweetness lighting up your reward system while your mind quietly recalls safe, cherished moments — that creates the cozy warmth you experience.
